problem_markdown: Two pentagons have vertices $A_1,\ldots,A_5$ and $B_1,\ldots,B_5$. Colour their ten sides and every segment $A_iB_j$ red or green. If no triangle whose three sides are coloured is monochromatic, prove the ten pentagon sides share one colour.
solutions_markdown:
If two sides at $A_1$ had different colours, choose three $B$-vertices joined to $A_1$ in one colour, say red, and let $A_1A_2$ be red. All three joins from $A_2$ must be green. Among three vertices of a pentagon two are adjacent. Their connecting side would form a monochromatic triangle with either $A_1$ or $A_2$, regardless of its colour. Thus the $A$-pentagon is monochromatic; the same argument applies to $B$.

Suppose their colours differ, say the $A$ sides are red and the $B$ sides green. Each $A_i$ can have at most two green joins to $B$, because three would include adjacent $B$-vertices and give a green triangle. Hence each of $A_1,A_2$ has at least three red joins. Their two three-element neighbour sets intersect, producing a red triangle with side $A_1A_2$. This contradiction proves both pentagons have the same colour.
